claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an intrinsic hierarchical heterostructure.
The initial material is bulk HfNbTiVAl10 produced with a controlled hierarchical heterostructure that was previously reported.
The proposed ML framework will use grain-boundary characteristics, phase distributions, and heterogeneity metrics as inputs.
The proposed framework will map microstructural descriptors directly to mechanical-property responses.
Hierarchical feature distributions, engineered grain boundaries, and phase architectures govern local stress distributions.
Hierarchical feature distributions, engineered grain boundaries, and phase architectures govern crack-initiation sites.
An ML model supplied with direct microstructural inputs can capture the essential physics controlling elastic deformation.
An ML model supplied with direct microstructural inputs can capture the essential physics controlling inelastic deformation.
Learning nonlinear relationships between microstructure and macroscopic performance permits rapid estimation of mechanical properties.
The ML approach bypasses computationally heavy and often oversimplified assumptions in conventional simulations.
The ML model will improve the predictive accuracy for Young’s modulus and yield strength by approximately 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The ML model will reduce computational time by approximately 50% relative to conventional simulations.
The ML model will delineate crack-initiation and crack-propagation thresholds under tensile loading.
Conventional continuum-mechanics and atomistic simulations require extensive computational resources.
Conventional simulations generally have prediction uncertainties exceeding ±5% for mechanical-property estimates.
Incomplete or inaccurate microstructural characterization may cause the proposed approach to fail.
Testing at temperatures or strain rates substantially outside the ML training domain may cause mechanical-response misestimation.
The accuracy and efficiency gains depend on descriptor fidelity and the representativeness of the training data.

Failure to achieve both at least a 20% accuracy improvement and a 50% computational-cost reduction relative to established simulations across multiple independent sample sets and testing conditions will falsify the hypothesis.
